Chapter 7: The Role of Curiosity in Relationships
You know, curiosity isn’t just about exploring the world out there. It’s also the secret ingredient that helps us truly understand the people closest to us. Whether we’re talking about friends, partners, or colleagues, relationships really come alive when we’re willing to ask questions, listen closely, and wonder about each other.
Picture this: a couple who’s been together for years. They know each other’s routines, favorite foods—maybe even those little pet peeves. But one evening, over a quiet dinner, one of them asks, “What’s something you’ve never told me?” There’s no pressure in the question—it’s gentle, a simple invitation. Suddenly, a new door opens. The conversation that follows? It’s full of surprises—maybe old dreams, hidden fears, even small joys that hadn’t come up before. They both leave the table feeling seen in a brand new way.
Most of us think we know the people around us pretty well, but honestly, we usually just skim the surface. It’s so easy to fall into routines—predicting each other’s reactions, finishing sentences, or assuming we know what someone’s thinking. But when you pause and ask, “How are you, really?” or “What’s on your mind these days?”—that’s when people feel cared for. You’re saying, “I want to know the real you, not just the version I’ve built up in my head.”
And curiosity at work? That can totally change a team’s dynamic. Imagine a manager who asks their team, “What do you need to do your best work?” or “Is there something you wish I understood about your job?” Suddenly, people feel valued for their perspective—not just for what they produce. Issues get solved faster, and trust starts to grow.
Curiosity is just as powerful when things get tense. Let’s face it, when conflict pops up, it’s tempting to defend yourself, argue, or just check out. But sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is ask, “Can you help me understand how you’re feeling?” or “What’s really important to you right now?” These questions won’t make disagreements disappear, but they do soften things. They remind everyone there’s always more to the story.
Think about a parent, frustrated because their child has gone quiet. Instead of pushing, they gently ask, “Is there something you wish I’d ask you about?” The child, maybe caught off guard, opens up about worries at school. Sure, it doesn’t solve everything, but it’s a start—a bridge between them.
Curiosity, when it comes to relationships, is a practice. It’s about showing up with openness and humility, over and over again. It means being okay with not having all the answers, being willing to be surprised, and listening without rushing in to fix things. Over time, these little acts of wonder build connections that are deeper, stronger, and honestly, a whole lot more joyful.
